provenance.basis: Independent skill briefs; no examination question supplied for paraphrasing.
provenance.verification: See docs/quadratics-original-20261030.md for checks actually performed.

marking_policy: Maths4U indicative marking guidance, not an official examination-board mark scheme. Award stated criteria once each, up to the part maximum. Accept valid equivalent methods. Follow-through applies only where explicitly stated; do not award an accuracy criterion for an incorrect final result.

lessons.title: Factorisation and valid roots
lessons.objective: Rearrange to zero, factorise and check every root against the original domain.
lessons.notes_html:
For a quadratic \(ax^2+bx+c=0\), \(a\ne0\), the zero-product rule applies after one side is zero. If \(uv=0\), then \(u=0\) or \(v=0\).

For \(a=1\), find two numbers with sum \(b\) and product \(c\). For a non-unit coefficient, split the middle term using a product \(ac\), then group terms. Check by expansion.

Never divide by an expression that could be zero without checking that case. A root of a rearranged equation is valid only if the original expression is defined.

examples.solution_html: Numbers with sum \(-1\) and product \(-20\) are \(-5,4\). Hence \((x-5)(x+4)=0\), so \(x=5,-4\).

examples.question_html: Solve \(x(x-4)=0\), explaining why division by \(x\) is unsafe.
examples.solution_html: The factors give \(x=0\) or \(x=4\). Dividing by \(x\) assumes \(x\ne0\) and loses the valid root zero.

common_mistakes: Putting each term equal to zero before obtaining a product.
Discarding zero by dividing by x.
Keeping a root that makes an original denominator zero.

lessons.title: Completing the square and range
lessons.objective: Transform a quadratic and interpret its vertex, range and intersections.
lessons.notes_html:
Since \((x+h)^2=x^2+2hx+h^2\), half the coefficient of \(x\) belongs inside the bracket. For \(a\ne0\),

\[ax^2+bx+c=a\left(x+\frac{b}{2a}\right)^2+c-\frac{b^2}{4a}.\]

Factor out \(a\) from the first two terms before completing the square. In \(a(x-h)^2+k\), the vertex is \((h,k)\). It is a minimum if \(a>0\) and a maximum if \(a<0\).

On a restricted domain, check whether the vertex is included and evaluate the endpoints. Solving an equation requires both square-root signs.

examples.solution_html: \(-3(x^2-4x)-5=-3(x-2)^2+7\). The square is nonnegative, so the maximum is \(7\) at \(x=2\).

examples.question_html: Find the range of \(2(x-1)^2+3\) for \(2\le x\le4\).
examples.solution_html: The vertex \(x=1\) is outside the domain. The function increases here; endpoint values are \(5\) and \(21\). The range is \(5\le y\le21\).

common_mistakes: Forgetting to multiply the compensation term by a.
Reading the sign of the vertex incorrectly.
Using the unrestricted minimum on a domain that excludes the vertex.

lessons.title: The discriminant and parameter conditions
lessons.objective: Translate root and tangency conditions into inequalities, retaining all necessary restrictions.
lessons.notes_html:
For real coefficients and \(a\ne0\), the discriminant is \(\Delta=b^2-4ac\). A positive value gives two distinct real roots, zero gives a repeated real root, and a negative value gives no real roots.

The roots satisfy \(\alpha+\beta=-b/a\) and \(\alpha\beta=c/a\). Two distinct positive roots require \(\Delta>0\), a positive sum and a positive product. A positive discriminant alone does not establish the signs.

To study intersections, equate the two expressions for \(y\). A tangent corresponds to a repeated intersection root. If a parameter can make \(a=0\), handle that linear case separately.

examples.question_html: How many real roots does \(2x^2+4x+5=0\) have?
examples.solution_html: \(\Delta=4^2-4(2)(5)=-24<0\), so there are no real roots.

examples.question_html: Find \(k\) if \(x^2-6x+k=0\) has a repeated root.
examples.solution_html: \(36-4k=0\) gives \(k=9\). The equation is \((x-3)^2=0\), with repeated root \(3\).

examples.question_html: For which \(r\) does \(x^2-4x+r=0\) have two distinct positive roots?
examples.solution_html: The discriminant gives \(r<4\). The sum is \(4>0\); the product requires \(r>0\). Together, \(0

common_mistakes: Using a non-strict inequality when roots must be distinct.
Treating two real roots as necessarily positive.
Ignoring a parameter value that turns a quadratic into a linear equation.

lessons.title: Quadratic inequalities and integer constraints
lessons.objective: Use roots and signs to find intervals, then impose additional constraints.
lessons.notes_html:
First rearrange the inequality so that one side is zero. Locate its real roots and determine the sign on each interval. For a quadratic with positive leading coefficient and two distinct roots, it is negative between the roots and positive outside.

Include a root for \(\le\) or \(\ge\), and exclude it for \(<\) or \(>\). With a negative leading coefficient, reverse the sign pattern. A repeated root does not change the sign.

Intersect the solution set with every domain restriction. If the variable counts objects, list only integers in the resulting interval. Multiplying by an unknown-sign expression can reverse an inequality; split cases instead.

examples.solution_html: \((x-3)(x+2)<0\). The upward-opening quadratic is negative between its roots: \(-2
Equivalently \((x-5)(x+1)\le0\), so \(-1\le x\le5\). Multiplication by \(-1\) reverses the inequality.

examples.question_html: An integer \(n\ge0\) satisfies \((n-2)(n-6)\le0\). List its values.
examples.solution_html: The real interval is \(2\le n\le6\). The allowable integers are \(2,3,4,5,6\), including both endpoints.

common_mistakes: Reporting only the roots instead of an interval.
Using closed endpoints for a strict inequality.
Forgetting the integer or domain restriction.

lessons.title: Linear and quadratic simultaneous equations
lessons.objective: Substitute, solve and reconstruct all coordinate pairs; recognise a tangent.
lessons.notes_html:
A linear equation lets you express one variable in terms of the other. Substitute into the quadratic, simplify to zero and solve. Then use the linear equation to recover the matching second coordinate for each root.

Check each pair in both original equations. Do not combine the first coordinate of one solution with the second coordinate of another.

The resulting quadratic describes the intersections. Two distinct roots give two points, a repeated root gives one tangent point, and no real roots mean no real intersection.

examples.solution_html: Substitution gives \(5x^2=45\), so \(x=\pm3\). The matched pairs are \((3,6)\), \((-3,-6)\).
\(x^2-4x+4=(x-2)^2=0\). There is one repeated intersection at \((2,4)\), so the line is tangent.

common_mistakes: Claiming a tangent without showing a repeated intersection root.

problems.title: Factors, roots and a cancelled denominator
problems.objective: Factor a non-monic quadratic and distinguish a cancelled expression from its domain.
problems.hint_html: Try factors with leading terms \(3x\) and \(2x\). Cancellation does not remove a restriction from the original denominator.

parts.prompt_html: Factorise \(f(x)\) completely.

criteria.requirement: Use a valid middle-term split or consistent pair of linear factors.

parts.alternative_methods: Any correct factorisation method, including finding roots then checking expansion.
parts.common_error: An incorrect sign in a constant factor.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Hence solve \(f(x)=0\).
parts.solution_html: Set each factor equal to zero: \(3x+4=0\) or \(2x-3=0\).

criteria.requirement: Apply the zero-product rule to both factors.

parts.alternative_methods: Quadratic formula with both correct roots also earns full credit.
parts.common_error: Dividing by one factor and losing its root.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: State the excluded value of \(x\) in \(\frac{f(x)}{3x+4}=1\), then solve this equation.
parts.solution_html: The original denominator requires \(x\ne-4/3\). For allowed values, the equation becomes \(2x-3=1\), so \(x=2\), which is allowed.

criteria.requirement: Reduce to \(2x-3=1\) on the permitted domain.

parts.alternative_methods: Multiplication followed by factorisation is valid if the excluded root is rejected.
parts.common_error: Accepting the excluded denominator root.
parts.label: c

problems.title: A rectangular display
problems.objective: Build and solve a quadratic model, rejecting a nonphysical root.
problems.stem_html: A rectangular display has width \(x\) metres and length \((2x+3)\) metres, where \(x>0\). Its area is \(35\text{ m}^2\).
problems.hint_html: Area is length times width. Test both algebraic roots against \(x>0\).

parts.prompt_html: Show that \(2x^2+3x-35=0\).
parts.solution_html: Multiply width by length: \(x(2x+3)=35\). Expanding and subtracting 35 gives the required equation.
parts.alternative_methods: An annotated expression for length times width is sufficient.
parts.common_error: Using perimeter instead of area.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find the width and length of the display.

criteria.requirement: Correctly solve the quadratic, obtaining both algebraic roots.
Reject the negative root and state width 3.5 m.

parts.alternative_methods: Quadratic formula followed by the domain check is accepted.
parts.common_error: Reporting both roots as dimensions.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Find the perimeter of the display.

criteria.requirement: Use twice the sum of the two dimensions.
Obtain 27 m; follow through positive dimensions from part (b) for method credit.

parts.alternative_methods: Adding all four side lengths is accepted.
parts.common_error: Giving square metres as the perimeter unit.
parts.label: c

problems.title: A minimum and a family of intersections
problems.objective: Complete the square and derive a parameter condition and exact intersection roots.
problems.hint_html: Factor 3 from the first two terms. Compare the horizontal level \(k\) with the vertex height.

parts.prompt_html: Write \(g(x)\) as \(a(x-h)^2+j\).

criteria.requirement: Factor 3 from the quadratic and linear terms.
Use the shift x−3 with the correct compensation.

parts.alternative_methods: Coefficient comparison or expansion of a proposed square is valid.
parts.common_error: Subtracting 9 rather than 27 from the original constant.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: State the minimum value and the value of \(x\) where it occurs.
parts.solution_html: Since \(3(x-3)^2\ge0\), the least value is 8, attained when the square is zero, at \(x=3\).

criteria.requirement: State minimum 8 using nonnegativity of the square.

parts.alternative_methods: A derivative with a valid minimum justification is accepted.
parts.common_error: Confusing the x-coordinate with the minimum value.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Find the values of real \(k\) for which \(g(x)=k\) has two distinct real roots, and give those roots in terms of \(k\).
parts.solution_html: The equation is \((x-3)^2=(k-8)/3\). Two distinct real roots require a positive right side: \(k>8\). Taking both signs gives \(x=3\pm\sqrt{(k-8)/3}\). At k=8 the root is repeated.

criteria.requirement: Give both exact roots with the square root covering (k−8)/3.

parts.alternative_methods: The discriminant gives the same condition; the quadratic formula may give equivalent roots.
parts.common_error: Including k=8 among the two-distinct-root cases.
parts.label: c

problems.title: A downward parabola on a restricted domain
problems.objective: Interpret a maximum, exact intercepts and the range on a closed interval.
problems.hint_html: Complete the square with a negative leading coefficient. For the restricted range, compare the vertex and both endpoints.

parts.prompt_html: Complete the square and state the coordinates of the maximum point.
parts.solution_html: \(-2(x^2-6x)-11=-2[(x-3)^2-9]-11=-2(x-3)^2+7\). The nonpositive square term is largest at zero, giving (3,7).

criteria.requirement: Obtain the completed form with constant 7.

parts.alternative_methods: Differentiation may locate the point but the requested completed form is still required.
parts.common_error: Treating the vertex as a minimum despite the negative coefficient.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Solve \(h(x)\ge0\), giving exact endpoints.
parts.solution_html: \(-2(x-3)^2+7\ge0\) gives \((x-3)^2\le7/2\). Thus \(-\sqrt{7/2}\le x-3\le\sqrt{7/2}\), giving the stated closed interval.

criteria.requirement: Give the interval between them with inclusive endpoints.

parts.alternative_methods: Equivalent endpoints 3±√(7/2), or a quadratic-formula and sign argument, are accepted.
parts.common_error: Using the exterior intervals or strict endpoints.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Find the range of \(h(x)\) when \(0\le x\le4\).
parts.solution_html: The vertex x=3 is included, so the maximum is 7. The endpoint values are h(0)=−11 and h(4)=5. The minimum is −11; continuity gives the full interval [−11,7].

criteria.requirement: Compare the included vertex and both endpoints.

parts.alternative_methods: Monotonicity on each side of x=3 plus endpoint values is accepted.
parts.common_error: Using the unrestricted lower bound of negative infinity.
parts.label: c

problems.title: Two roots are not always two positive roots
problems.objective: Combine discriminant, root sum and root product conditions.
problems.hint_html: Factor the discriminant as an expression in p. Then use the sum and product to control the signs of the roots.

parts.prompt_html: Find all \(p\) for which the equation has two distinct real roots.
parts.solution_html: \(\Delta=4p^2-4p-24=4(p-3)(p+2)\). Two distinct real roots require \((p-3)(p+2)>0\), giving p<−2 or p>3.

criteria.requirement: Factor or locate the boundary values −2 and 3.
Give the two strict exterior intervals.

parts.alternative_methods: Completing the square in p or solving the discriminant inequality by another valid method is accepted.
parts.common_error: Taking the interval between the discriminant roots.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find each value of \(p\) that gives a repeated root, and state that root.
parts.solution_html: Set the discriminant to zero: p=−2 or p=3. The repeated root is −b/(2a)=p. The equations become (x+2)²=0 and (x−3)²=0 respectively.

criteria.requirement: Match each parameter to its repeated root.

parts.alternative_methods: Direct factorisation for each parameter is accepted.
parts.common_error: Listing the repeated roots without the matching parameter values.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Find all \(p\) for which the equation has two distinct positive roots. Justify your answer.
parts.solution_html: The sum is 2p and the product is p+6. Positivity requires p>0 and p>−6. Intersecting these with part (a) leaves p>3. Conversely, for p>3 both roots are real, their product is positive and their sum is positive, so both are positive.

criteria.requirement: Use positive product p+6>0 together with distinct real roots.
Intersect to p>3 and justify sufficiency.

parts.alternative_methods: Analysing the signs of the exact roots is accepted if complete.
parts.common_error: Assuming every real-root case has positive roots.
parts.label: c

problems.title: Two tangents through a fixed point
problems.objective: Form an intersection equation and find both tangent gradients and points.
problems.stem_html: The curve is \(y=x^2+2x+4\). A line through \((0,1)\) has equation \(y=mx+1\).
problems.hint_html: At tangency the intersection quadratic has a repeated root. Do not discard either sign of the gradient.

parts.prompt_html: Show that an intersection has x-coordinate satisfying \(x^2+(2-m)x+3=0\).
parts.solution_html: Equate the two expressions for y and collect all terms on the left.
parts.alternative_methods: Substituting the line expression into the curve equation is equivalent.
parts.common_error: Using a constant term 5 instead of 3.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find both values of \(m\) for which the line is tangent.
parts.solution_html: A repeated root requires (2−m)²−12=0. Thus m−2=±2√3, so m=2±2√3.

criteria.requirement: Set the discriminant equal to zero.

parts.alternative_methods: Using the derivative at x=t and the fixed-point condition is accepted.
parts.common_error: Keeping only the positive square-root branch.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Find the point of contact for each gradient.
parts.solution_html: The repeated root is x=(m−2)/2. Hence x=√3 for the plus branch and x=−√3 for the minus branch. Substitution into the curve gives y=7±2√3, with the signs matched.

criteria.requirement: Use x=(m−2)/2 or an equivalent repeated-root calculation.
Give correctly matched points and gradients.

parts.alternative_methods: Substitution into the corresponding tangent line is equally valid.
parts.common_error: Mixing the signs of the coordinates or tangent gradients.
parts.label: c

problems.title: Intersecting two quadratic conditions
problems.objective: Solve a non-monic inequality and combine strict and inclusive boundaries.
problems.stem_html: A real number \(x\) must satisfy both \(2x^2-5x-3\le0\) and \(x^2-4>0\).
problems.hint_html: Solve each inequality separately, draw their intervals on a number line, then take the overlap.

parts.prompt_html: Find the roots of \(2x^2-5x-3=0\).
parts.solution_html: \(2x^2-5x-3=(2x+1)(x-3)\), so the roots are −1/2 and 3.
parts.alternative_methods: Any valid exact-root method is accepted.
parts.common_error: A sign error in the smaller root.
parts.label: a

parts.solution_html: The leading coefficient is positive, so the expression is nonpositive between its roots, including both endpoints.

criteria.requirement: Choose the interval between the roots using a sign argument.

parts.alternative_methods: A sign table or upward-parabola argument is accepted.
parts.common_error: Selecting the exterior intervals.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Hence find all \(x\) satisfying both original inequalities.
parts.solution_html: The second inequality gives x<−2 or x>2. Its intersection with [−1/2,3] is (2,3]. The endpoint 2 is excluded; 3 is allowed.

criteria.requirement: Obtain x<−2 or x>2 for the second condition.
Intersect correctly, with 2 excluded and 3 included.

parts.alternative_methods: A clear number-line overlap is sufficient.
parts.common_error: Taking a union instead of the intersection.
parts.label: c

problems.title: An integer setting for a display
problems.objective: Combine a quadratic threshold with an integer domain and optimise.
problems.stem_html: A display setting \(n\) is an integer with \(0\le n\le15\). Its score is modelled by \(C(n)=-n^2+14n+15\).
problems.hint_html: Rearrange C(n)≥60 before factorising. Use completed-square form for the largest possible score.

parts.prompt_html: Find the real values of \(n\) for which \(C(n)\ge60\).
parts.solution_html: −n²+14n+15≥60 is equivalent to n²−14n+45≤0. This factors as (n−5)(n−9)≤0, so 5≤n≤9.

criteria.requirement: Rearrange with the correct inequality direction.

parts.alternative_methods: Completing the square to (n−7)²≤4 is accepted.
parts.common_error: Failing to reverse the inequality when multiplying by −1.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: List all permitted settings that give a score of at least 60.
parts.solution_html: Intersect [5,9] with the integer domain 0≤n≤15. The five allowable settings are 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9.

criteria.requirement: List exactly the five settings, including both boundary settings.

parts.alternative_methods: Integer set notation with the same five values is accepted.
parts.common_error: Including noninteger settings or omitting 5 and 9.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Find the greatest possible score and the setting giving it.
parts.solution_html: C(n)=−(n−7)²+64. The maximum is 64 at n=7, which is a permitted integer setting.

criteria.requirement: Use a valid maximum method and check the setting is permitted.

parts.alternative_methods: Symmetry, differentiation with the domain check, or a complete integer comparison is accepted.
parts.common_error: Reporting the setting as the score.
parts.label: c

problems.title: A line crossing a circle
problems.objective: Solve a line–circle system and use paired coordinates to find a chord length.
problems.stem_html: The line \(y=x+2\) meets the circle \(x^2+y^2=20\) at points \(A\) and \(B\).
problems.hint_html: Substitute the line into the circle. Match each y-value with its own x-value before finding the distance.

parts.prompt_html: Show that the x-coordinates satisfy \(x^2+2x-8=0\).
parts.solution_html: Expanding gives 2x²+4x+4=20. Rearrange and divide by 2 to obtain x²+2x−8=0.

criteria.requirement: Substitute y=x+2 into the circle correctly.
Expand and simplify to the required equation.

parts.alternative_methods: Eliminating x instead of y is valid if the requested x-equation is recovered.
parts.common_error: Expanding (x+2)² as x²+4.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find the coordinates of \(A\) and \(B\).
parts.solution_html: (x+4)(x−2)=0, so x=−4 or x=2. Using y=x+2 gives (−4,−2) and (2,4). Each satisfies the circle equation.
parts.alternative_methods: The quadratic formula and substitution are accepted.
parts.common_error: Matching −4 with 4 or 2 with −2.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Find the exact length \(AB\).

criteria.requirement: Apply the distance formula to the two points.
Simplify to 6√2; method credit may follow through two distinct points from part (b).

parts.alternative_methods: Pythagoras using horizontal and vertical differences 6 and 6 is accepted.
parts.common_error: Adding coordinate differences instead of their squares.
parts.label: c

problems.title: Moving a parallel line
problems.objective: Find a tangent intercept and compare with a nearby secant.
problems.stem_html: The curve is \(y=x^2-3x+1\). The parallel family of lines is \(y=2x+c\), where \(c\) is real.
problems.hint_html: Equating y-values gives a quadratic whose discriminant depends on c. Recover y after finding the repeated x-value.

parts.prompt_html: Find the value of \(c\) for which the line is tangent to the curve.
parts.solution_html: Intersections satisfy x²−5x+1−c=0. Tangency requires 25−4(1−c)=21+4c=0, so c=−21/4.

criteria.requirement: Set its discriminant equal to zero.

parts.alternative_methods: Completing the square or matching the derivative to 2 is accepted.
parts.common_error: Using the discriminant of the curve before subtracting the line.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find the point of contact.
parts.solution_html: The repeated root is x=5/2. On the tangent, y=2(5/2)−21/4=−1/4. The point is (5/2,−1/4).

criteria.requirement: Substitute to give the paired coordinate (5/2,−1/4).

parts.alternative_methods: Substitution into the curve is accepted.
parts.common_error: Using the intercept c as the y-coordinate of contact.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: When \(c=-5\), find both intersection points and explain why the line is no longer tangent.
parts.solution_html: The intersection equation is x²−5x+6=(x−2)(x−3)=0. The points are (2,−1) and (3,1). There are two distinct roots (equivalently, discriminant 1>0), so the line is a secant.

criteria.requirement: Explain using two distinct roots or a positive discriminant why it is not tangent.

parts.alternative_methods: Any correct intersection method with a valid distinction from a repeated root is accepted.
parts.common_error: Assuming parallel lines must have the same number of intersections.
parts.label: c
